item.title: The Champion of chonk: Backpack takes the 2026 Fat Bear Week crown at Katmai National Park
item.description: Bear 89 Backpack defeated Bear 910 by just over 5,000 votes in the Fat Bear Week 2026 final at Alaska's Katmai National Park on Brooks River.
item.content:encoded:
We have a new king of Katmai.

Bear 89 — better known as Backpack — is the 2026 Fat Bear Week champion after defeating Bear 910 in Tuesday's final at Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

The people have spoken: He is the chonkiest. The chonk champion. The chonkion, if you will.

Backpack pulled in 103,334 votes to 98,253 for 910, capping a tournament that drew more than 2.3 million votes from around the world.

And apparently, winning runs in the family.

Backpack is the son of Bear 435, Holly, who won Fat Bear Week in 2019. As a cub, he had a habit of climbing onto his mother's back while the pair crossed Brooks River — hence the nickname.

WILDLIFE PHOTOGRAPHER STAYS ICE-COLD AS MASSIVE BROWN BEAR WALKS RIGHT UP TO HIS CAMERA

His early years weren't exactly easy, either.

As a yearling in 2007, Backpack suffered a serious leg injury and spent much of the summer unable to put weight on it. At the time, park staff and visitors weren't sure he would survive.

But the leg healed, Backpack stuck around, and over the years he became a familiar face at Brooks Falls.

Now, at about 20 years old, he's got a Fat Bear Week title of his own.

This year’s competition was stacked.

Backpack crushed Bear 620 with more than 95% of the vote in the second round, then barely survived a semifinal showdown with Bear 164, Bucky, 79,945 votes to 75,805.

Then came 910, who had already knocked off Bear 909 and the 132 family on her way to the final.

Backpack won that one by a little more than 5,000 votes.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

And now he gets to celebrate the same way he would have anyway. By sitting in a river, eating as much salmon as physically possible and eventually disappearing for a long winter nap.

Oh, to be a bear.

item.title: Texas A&M posts blank end zone teaser on social media, internet trolls understand their assignment
item.description: Texas A&M football's social media team posted a blank end zone graphic that became an open canvas for internet trolls after the Aggies' 2-2 start.
item.content:encoded:
Posting on social media for a big corporation is a tightrope act these days.

You want to create an engaging post, but you don't want something low hanging that will cause internet trolls to come out of the woods and take pot shots at.

It's even crazier for a high-level college football team, because fans of every other team are just looking for a reason to roast you into oblivion.

As a former social media manager, I don't envy the position these people are in.

FSU FOOTBALL X ACCOUNT GETS COMMUNITY NOTED FOR CLAIMING 'RECORD GPA' IN SOCIAL MEDIA POST

With all that said, the social media team for Texas A&M's football program posted what is perhaps the greatest opportunity for any internet troll with access to Photoshop that has existed in quite some time.

To the uninitiated, this may just look like a team hyping up their new end zones for Saturday, but to "students of the game," this is basically a blank canvas for trolling opportunities.

Don't believe me? Observe.

FALCONS' TUA TAGOVAILOA GETS ROASTED ON SOCIAL MEDIA AFTER ALLEGEDLY COMMENTING ON HIS OWN POST

You know, if the Aggies were 4-0 right now, this probably wouldn't be going as poorly in the comments section.

But the fact that A&M is 2-2 and reeling after back to back losses to Kentucky and LSU made this almost too easy to see coming.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

You just don't get opportunities like this anymore as digital graffiti artists, mainly because social media managers have been around the block a few times before, so I have no idea how anyone on the Aggies' social media team let this one slip through the cracks.

They even left the generic blank Photoshop fill on the end zones, almost as if they wanted this to happen.

Was this a false flag operation by Texas A&M to generate engagement?

I doubt it.

Like I said, this was a top-ten preseason team with College Football Playoff aspirations that is now sitting at 2-2 and on the brink of missing the big dance entirely.

I'm sure their posts are being engaged with plenty, though most of that engagement is coming from angry Aggie fans demanding to know why Marcel Reed is still allowed to touch a football.

I think this was just a rookie mistake committed by whoever is in charge of the phones in College Station.

Let this be a lesson to anyone hiring a social media manager for a big-time sports team or Fortune 500 company.

Be careful who you give access to the "nuclear codes."

item.title: Prime Video WNBA broadcast crew embarrasses itself with coverage of A'ja Wilson fan incident
item.description: Prime Video's panel blamed an Indiana Fever fan after A'ja Wilson's confrontation, but arena security found no Fan Code of Conduct violation.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Video's coverage of Tuesday's Aces-Fever playoff game came with a remarkably simple explanation for A'ja Wilson's confrontation with a fan: Wilson was upset, so the fan must have done something wrong.

The Fever, however, said arena security spoke with the fan and witnesses and found no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct. The team's statement never made it into Prime's postgame discussion.

ACES' A'JA WILSON GETS TECH FOR CONFRONTATION WITH FEVER FAN, WHO WAS DETERMINED TO HAVE BROKEN NO RULES

"Following a report of a comment directed toward a player, arena security spoke with the fan involved and witnesses. Security determined there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct, the fan was not removed from the arena. We consider the matter closed," the team said.

A nearby spectator told OutKick the fan was disputing the foul call while pointing at Wilson.

Wilson received a technical foul after the fourth-quarter confrontation during Indiana's 99-89 victory, which tied the series at one game apiece. Prime's broadcasters immediately defended her reaction without establishing what the fan had done to warrant it.

Following the incident, color analyst Candace Parker acknowledged, "We don't know what was said." But that didn't stop fellow analyst LaChina Robinson from describing Wilson's reaction as "not even in line with her demeanor unless it's absolutely necessary."

Absolutely necessary? How could Robinson know that from watching Wilson react?

And it's not as if there was no context available, either.

Watching live, I noticed an arena security guard seated directly in front of the fan. He didn't react or stand up until Wilson had aggressively crossed the baseline, and the fan was already seated by then.

One might think a security guard sitting directly in front of a fan would intervene if he heard something inappropriate or saw the fan enter an area where he wasn't allowed. That would have been useful context for the broadcast to note. Instead, the broadcast treated Wilson's reaction as the only one that mattered.

Play-by-play announcer Michael Grady described the stoppage as officials clearing things up and getting "this fan out of the building." The fan was not removed from the arena, according to the Fever.

Parker also invoked previous incidents, saying, "I feel like this has happened several times here in Indiana."

Well, previous complaints about Indiana fans haven't always held up under investigation.

In August, after Aces guard Jackie Young complained about a fan during a game in Indiana, the Fever said security found no Fan Code of Conduct violation. The team said that fan was not removed from the arena but elected to leave.

ACES STAR TARGETS HECKLING FEVER FANS IN INDY BEFORE CHELSEA GRAY STUNS CAITLIN CLARK IN OT THRILLER

Last year, the WNBA investigated allegations of racist behavior by Fever fans toward Angel Reese and said those allegations were not substantiated. In that case, it was ESPN rushing to embrace those allegations before the investigation was complete.

Parker didn't identify which incidents she meant. But prior complaints don't become proof of fan misconduct just because a broadcaster brings them up again.

By the postgame show, Prime had more time to gather information. Lindsey Harding instead offered viewers certainty based on her familiarity with Wilson.

"I know something was said. Something was said, disrespectful, to a point for her to do that, and it's not okay," Harding said.

OK, what was it?

Harding didn't identify the comment. She went on to say, "It's always a player that gets attacked and has to stand up for themselves. And you know what? She stood up for herself, and she got a technical foul for that."

Harding described Wilson as defending herself without establishing that the fan attacked her.

Swin Cash also relied on Wilson's character, telling viewers, "So whatever was said, whether it was pointing, something happened."

Teresa Weatherspoon referred to "the words that were possibly said" before telling the fan to "back that crap up and sit down."

Host Allie Clifton responded, "Well said by all three of you," without pushing back on any of them, even though all three made claims that deserved further inspection.

Clifton then clarified that the fan remained in the arena and was not ejected. But the discussion never addressed security's finding that he had not violated the Fan Code of Conduct.

The Fever's statement was circulating on X by 8:53 p.m. ET, roughly 15 minutes before Prime's postgame discussion began.

Prime then aired part of Wilson's explanation, which focused on the fan's movements and pointing.

"I don't give a damn what you said. I don't give a damn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable," Wilson said.

Wilson was describing her objection to a "man" stepping toward her. Her account did not support Harding's claim that the fan had made a disrespectful comment. Nor does a player's objection to being pointed at establish that a fan broke arena rules.

Cash responded to the clip by saying, "Now, there may have been other things that were said and whatnot."

Oh, OK. Wilson focused on the fan stepping toward her and pointing, but Cash still wanted to speculate about "other things" he might have said. What information supported that speculation?

They also didn't take Wilson to task for escalating the exchange, overreacting to standard sports fan behavior, and costing her team a technical foul at a crucial late-game moment.

CAITLIN CLARK'S TECHNICAL FOUL SPARKS FURIOUS RALLY AS FEVER AVOID ELIMINATION AGAINST ACES

Of the seven Prime broadcasters, not one raised the most likely explanation: Wilson was frustrated with the way the game was going and took it out on a fan. She had dominated Game 1 with 38 points and 16 rebounds. At the time of the confrontation in Game 2, she had 14 points and the Aces trailed by 11 with 4:10 remaining.

Indiana fans have become an easy scapegoat, and the reaction on Bluesky showed how little information some people needed to blame them. One user wrote, "I don't really care what the fan said. If it upset Wilson that much, toss him." Another demanded that Wilson's technical be rescinded and blamed "racist bastards."

I wouldn't be surprised if Wilson expected people around the WNBA to rush to her defense in a confrontation with a Fever fan. Prime's panel certainly obliged.

And for all the talk about diversity in sports television, where was the diversity of thought? Prime's seven broadcasters included five Black women, one Black man and one White woman, yet nobody in the game or postgame discussion challenged the assumption that the fan must have done something wrong.

Seven different people reached roughly the same conclusion because that's what happens when "diversity" means "not White men" instead of diversity of thought.

OutKick asked the Fever whether the guard seated in front of the fan was among the witnesses security interviewed and what its review established about the fan's words and movements. We also asked when the team provided its findings to Prime. The Fever did not respond to those follow-up questions before publication.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

OutKick asked Prime to explain the reporting behind its commentators' assertions and account for its handling of the Fever's statement. Prime did not respond before publication.

Seeking the Fever's account was a basic reporting obligation.

The panel spent several minutes condemning a fan without presenting arena security’s finding that the fan had not violated the conduct code. That's a complete dereliction of journalistic duty.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Harding told viewers, "I know."

It's pretty easy to "know" when you've decided the outcome without needing to see any proof.

item.title: Trump DOJ investigating Dem group in Texas after viral undercover video sparks massive uproar
item.description: A viral undercover video showing a Texas Majority PAC employee describing a "Paid Relational Program" has now triggered a DOJ investigation.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: A Texas PAC that dumps millions into Democrat campaigns in the Lone Star state is under a Department of Justice (DOJ) investigation following a viral undercover video featuring a now-former employee, two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to Fox News Digital.

"We are paying people $25 to attend a one hour Zoom class to learn why voting is important and why the Republicans are causing all these bad things," Sky McAdams, a former organizing manager at the Texas Majority PAC told an undercover reporter in a video obtained by Townhall.

"So it's like a roundabout way of paying people for their votes, essentially, which is interesting," said McAdams. When the undercover reporter asked what the program was called, McAdams said it's called the "Paid Relational Program."

"I think 'Rally Texas' is the official name," McAdams continued. "You can't pay someone to vote for someone. You can't be like, 'Here's $25, go vote for me.' You can say, 'attend a one hour class and you can receive $25,' and then the class just talks about, like, the importance of voting."

REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES

"It's a creative way to kind of... but right now we could use all the help we can get," the reporter says in response.

"Yeah, you know, like, if I was a Republican, I'd be pissed. I'd be like, 'that's shady as f---,'" McAdams agreed of the supposed nefarious-ness of the action in his reply.

The video has racked up millions of views online, leading to the DOJ probe into the Texas Majority PAC.

The Texas Majority PAC was founded by "veterans of Texas campaigns" Jason Lee, Katherine Fischer and Crystal Zermeño. The group's mission is to turn Texas permanently blue. According to Transparency USA, by the end of Q2, the PAC had raised nearly $10 million in the 2026 election cycle, and has spent nearly $9 million. It reportedly had more than $1.3 million in cash on hand.

A spokesperson for the PAC, Eddie Vale, told Fox News Digital that the video is real and has not been digitally altered or deceptively edited. He also clarified details about "relational organizing" program described by McAdams in the video.

TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS

"We hire Texans to join events where they are taught how to organize their friends and family.," he said. "They encourage their friends and family to turn out and vote and send them regular reminders. They are compensated for their organizing work, just like any other job."

"Texas Majority PAC runs a relational organizing program, which for years has been a standard part of every campaign’s playbook," Vale said. "Participants in the program are being paid for grassroots organizing work. The way it was described by one rogue employee is factually incorrect, not how we operate, and they were immediately fired."

"We will continue to ensure that everyone who has the legal right to vote is able to do so in the face of never-ending attempts from Texas Republicans to disenfranchise them and bad faith attacks from right-wing media to silence organizations that try to help them," Vale continued.

Meanwhile, Texas Democrats are feverishly attempting to rally support for scandal-plagued Senate candidate James Talarico.

The left-wing candidate has recently walked back some of his more extreme positions, like support for biological men in women's sports, his previous claims that "God is non-binary" and that there are six sexes.

Talarico is running against Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Despite the fact that Texas is known as a traditionally red state, the outcome could be decided by a razor thin margin.

Neither McAdams nor the Texas Majority PAC returned Fox News Digital's comment requests related to the investigation.

item.title: Explosive sleeper issue could fuel midterm shakeups, top Republican predicts: ‘You’re gonna see surprises’
item.description: Tom Emmer says fraud is the top issue driving Minnesota voters to the polls and predicts Republican "surprises" in several midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
LEWISTON, MAINE - With just about a month left until the midterm elections, Rep. Tom Emmer (R-MN) told Fox News Digital that fraud is an issue motivating voters to the polls, and in Minnesota, his home state, he thinks the issue could yield some "surprises" at the ballot box.

"Fraud is a lot more important to the U.S. taxpayers than being a Republican or a Democrat," Emmer said. "People want good government. They want to know that they're paying for good government, that they are not having their hard-earned taxpayer dollars being siphoned off and stolen and sent out of the country. They're also asking, why hasn't anyone called this out and held these people accountable? And I think you're going to see that at the ballot box on November 3."

Emmer, the House Majority Whip, was in Maine with Republican House candidate Paul LePage, the first stop of his planned 56-district nationwide blitz across the United States, rallying voters for Republicans as the party tries to hold on their razor-thin majority in the House against daunting historical and political headwinds.

Emmer’s home state of Minnesota was the epicenter of fraud’s explosion into the national conversation late last year, prompting Gov. Tim Walz to abandon his re-election bid. Emmer expressed optimism that Republicans in Minnesota will resonate with voters on fraud in a state where a Republican hasn’t won a statewide election since 2006.

KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?'

"Fraud in Minnesota is the number one issue," Emmer said. "We've got a completely incompetent, I would argue corrupt in some instances, governor and an attorney general who took campaign funds from Somali fraudsters that he was actively trying to protect from getting caught in their fraud. This is a big deal for Minnesotans."

Emmer said voters are looking for an "honest system that actually works for the people" and not "the criminals" and the Republican candidates for Senate, governor, attorney general and auditor in Minnesota have all made fighting fraud a central issue of their campaigns.

NEW AUDIT IN WALZ'S BACKYARD EXPOSES MASSIVE FRAUD RISK TIED TO POST-GEORGE FLOYD ACTIVISM

"You easily could have Michelle Tafoya being the next U.S. Senator from the state of Minnesota, a Republican, you could have Lisa Demuth as the Republican governor and already, the attorney general candidate, Ron Schutz and the state auditor candidate Scott Jensen, the polling showing that they are leading," Emmer said. "So yes, Minnesota is going to be one of those places where you see surprises. I think you're gonna see surprises in Michigan as well and other places all across the country."

Emmer sat down for a roundtable discussion on fraud with LePage, Maine’s former governor running for Congress in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, where the Minnesota Republican railed against the lack of accountability for fraud in his home state.

"They need to be held accountable and that's the one thing that's missing again in Minnesota. You've got all of these fraudsters being charged and convicted, not one public official has been charged at all, and that's got to change, and I hope it changes in Maine and other places, because it's high time that people be held accountable for ripping off the generous American people," Emmer told the panel.

The Trump administration has made combating fraud a central focus this year, creating a Justice Department Fraud Division and a White House task force led by Vice President JD Vance. The White House says the task force has uncovered roughly $245.7 billion in fraud since its creation, while also stopping an additional $62.9 billion annually and enforcing $59.1 billion through criminal charges, settlements and penalties.

item.title: Secret phone-record seizure sparks personal lawsuit from GOP senator
item.description: Marsha Blackburn's lawsuit targets Jack Smith personally, arguing the special counsel was never lawfully appointed and violated her constitutional rights.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A top Republican senator whose phone toll records were secretly subpoenaed during Jack Smith's investigation of President Donald Trump sued the former special counsel in his personal capacity Wednesday, arguing he was never lawfully empowered to wield the authority behind the Arctic Frost investigation.

The lawsuit, Senator Marsha Blackburn v. John L. Smith, argues the prosecutor lacked lawful authority to serve as special counsel and violated the lawmaker's rights by obtaining the records. Blackburn is asking a federal court to declare Smith's appointment unconstitutional, order the records destroyed and award $1 in nominal damages.

The case therefore seeks to test not only Smith’s tactics, but the legitimacy of the authority he claims to have exercised as special counsel appointed by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland during the Biden administration.

"This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation’s justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people," Blackburn, R-Tenn., told Fox News Digital.

JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION

"Through his Arctic Frost witch-hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the president of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation’s history," she said.

Blackburn’s suit argues that Smith lacked lawful authority to hold the office he purported to exercise, while separately seeking to impose personal liability on him for the way that purported authority was used against her.

JACK SMITH THRUST BACK INTO SPOTLIGHT AT BLANCHE HEARING OVER EXPOSED SENATORS’ MESSAGES

The case opens a new legal front against Smith one day after his contentious Senate Judiciary Committee testimony, during which he acknowledged approving subpoenas for members of Congress despite understanding that nondisclosure orders prevented them from challenging the seizures under the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause.

Smith is a longtime prosecutor who most recently served as special counsel overseeing the Justice Department's investigations into President Donald Trump. Earlier in his career, he prosecuted cases before the International Criminal Court and led the DOJ's Public Integrity Section, which brought bribery charges against former Virginia Republican Gov. Robert F. McDonnell in a case where the Supreme Court later unanimously vacated the conviction.

Arctic Frost was the codename for the FBI investigation into Trump's handling of classified documents and alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election before the probe was handed over to Smith by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland.

Blackburn and her data were swept up in the probe after Smith's team subpoenaed toll records from her and several other Republicans—a move that sparked outrage at Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing over whether obtaining the records without notification violated the Constitution.

In May 2023, Smith’s office issued a grand-jury subpoena seeking Verizon toll records, while a separate nondisclosure order barred the company from notifying affected customers—including Blackburn—that its information had been turned over.

While the records did not reveal the contents of conversations, they showed whom Blackburn communicated with, when and for how long, according to the complaint. The lawsuit alleges that Smith’s office obtained a court-approved nondisclosure order without informing the judge that the subpoena sought records belonging to a sitting U.S. senator.

JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS

More broadly, Smith’s team issued 197 subpoenas to 34 individuals and 163 businesses seeking information involving at least 430 Republican individuals and entities, according to Senate Judiciary Committee records.

Tuesday’s hearing also began with a scathing rebuke from Chairman Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, who accused Smith’s prosecutors of sweeping up communications between journalists at Fox News and other media organizations and sources connected to the first Trump administration.

For his part, Smith repeatedly hit back at allegations of corrupt or partisan prosecution, saying at one point his "investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation."

Blackburn's suit is being brought by the nonpartisan New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA) on her behalf, and the Tennessee senator thanked the group for its partnership.

JACK SMITH'S SENATE PHONE RECORDS PROBE TURNS TO VERIZON'S HANDLING OF SUBPOENAS

Blackburn’s attorneys argue that Smith exercised special counsel powers without lawful constitutional or statutory authorization. Separately, the complaint names Smith in his personal capacity and seeks to hold him liable for alleged violations of Blackburn’s constitutional and civil rights arising from the subpoena and nondisclosure order.

"Jack Smith was illegally named Special Counsel in November of 2022, with Attorney General Merrick Garland handing a private citizen the sweeping powers of a special counsel," NCLA said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

"Then-President Biden did not nominate Smith, nor did the Senate confirm Smith as either Special Counsel or in any other position. And no statute authorized his appointment."

"NCLA’s complaint asks the court to declare Smith’s appointment unlawful under the Constitution’s Appointments Clause and to hold Smith accountable, in his personal capacity, for his gross abuses of power."

VETERAN DEM BREAKS PARTY LINE AS JACK SMITH SPYING SCANDAL GRIPS CAPITOL HILL

The suit alleges the subpoena violated Blackburn’s constitutional and civil rights and that the nondisclosure order prevented her from challenging the demand under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause.

"This lawsuit is not only about the faux authority granted to Smith through an unconstitutional appointment. It is also about ensuring that the Department of Justice—the very body responsible for enforcing federal law on behalf of our nation—acts only within its constitutional bounds," NCLA counsel L. Margaret Harker said in a statement.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The lawsuit seeks a declaration that Smith's appointment was unconstitutional, the return and destruction of Blackburn's phone records, and $1 in nominal damages. NCLA says the limited damages request reflects Blackburn's stated goal of obtaining judicial accountability for what the complaint alleges were constitutional violations committed while Smith exercised special counsel powers.

Fox News Digital reached out to Smith's counsel for comment.

item.title: Mamdani’s antisemitism plan draws criticism as rabbis say it avoids key driver of hate
item.description: Three leading rabbis across Manhattan say they were never consulted on NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's antisemitism plan or how funding was allocated.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a multimillion-dollar strategy to combat antisemitism, drawing criticism from prominent Jewish leaders who described the announcement as an attempt to deflect attention from the mayor’s own rhetoric while avoiding one of the defining sources of modern anti-Jewish hostility: the demonization of Israel and Zionism.

Mamdani announced what his administration called the nation’s first municipal strategy dedicated to combating antisemitism, declaring that Jewish New Yorkers "should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America."

The mayor cited New York Police Department statistics showing that although Jewish residents constitute approximately 12% of the city’s population, antisemitic incidents account for more than half of its confirmed hate crimes.

EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN

"This is not only unacceptable, it’s something we all have an obligation to change," Mamdani said. "And City Hall will lead the way."

His administration said it is increasing hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, an increase of more than 800% from the previous year. The plan includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate violence and would restart an interagency security and infrastructure initiative disbanded in 2024.

The city also pledged $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture, alongside expanded education, reporting resources and security support for Jewish institutions.

The way that money would be distributed also drew scrutiny. Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, said that only $1 million is dedicated specifically to security while millions more would be directed through community initiatives.

MAMDANI IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER FIRST VETO DERAILS BIPARTISAN EFFORT TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM: 'DISAPPOINTED'

"All of this money is pure pork barrel politics," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "Outside of a million dollars in security, it is all being spent on community initiatives that will reward his supporters."

The Jewish leaders who spoke with Fox News Digital welcomed the security investments but argued that physical protection alone cannot address an environment in which Jews increasingly feel pressured to distance themselves from Israel.

From Manhattan’s East Side to its West Side, three prominent rabbis shared another concern: Not one had been contacted by the mayor or his administration while the strategy was being developed, despite collectively leading some of the borough’s largest Jewish congregations.

Those concerns raise basic questions about how the strategy was constructed: which Jewish leaders and institutions helped shape it, how did the administration decide where the funding would go, and how were organizations selected to receive it? Fox News Digital asked those questions, along with Steinmetz’s criticism of the funding process, to the mayor’s office but had not received a response at the time of publication.

The mayor's strategy acknowledges rising antisemitism since Oct. 7 and expands Holocaust education, but does not directly address the hostility Jewish students have experienced on college campuses or examine when anti-Israel activism crosses into antisemitic harassment and intimidation. The three rabbis interviewed by Fox News Digital identified that omission as a significant weakness in the city’s strategy.

Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch, senior rabbi of Stephen Wise Free Synagogue in Manhattan and president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the plan omits what he considers the central driver of contemporary antisemitism.

CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS

"If the purpose here is to combat and reduce antisemitism, the plan omits the central driver of contemporary antisemitism, which is an obsessive loathing of Israel," Hirsch told Fox News Digital.

That hostility, he said, is directed "not only" toward the state of Israel but toward "the Zionist idea, the right of Israel to exist, the right of the Jewish people to self-determination in the land of Israel."

"To write a 30-page report and never mention the state of Israel, let alone address the vicious anti-Zionism, partially fomented by the mayor himself, is evading the issue," Hirsch said. "It’s not dealing head-on with the issue itself."

ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS

Hirsch welcomed the additional security funding, while emphasizing that Jewish institutions must routinely absorb expenses other communities do not face.

"The security obligations in every Jewish institution in the city are, in effect, an additional surtax on New York Jews that nobody else pays," he said. "And so any funds for security are welcome."

He also supported educational initiatives and Holocaust museum visits but said the city must teach more than the history of Jewish persecution.

"What I would like to see is a focus in New York public schools on the nexus, the connection between anti-Zionism and antisemitism," Hirsch said.

"One of the key lessons from the Holocaust," he added, is that "Jewish self-determination and Jewish empowerment are the answer to Jewish powerlessness that gave rise to centuries of antisemitism that culminated in genocide."

Steinmetz also said the mayor is using the strategy to avoid examining the consequences of his own language.

"Rather than taking responsibility for combating antisemitism, Mamdani is using this plan to deflect attention from himself," Steinmetz said. "His rhetoric has been reckless."

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Steinmetz said statistics measuring physical crimes capture only part of what Jewish New Yorkers experience.

"Far more common is the nasty look and whispered insult," he said. "You cannot talk about a trip to Israel at the water cooler. Jews feel like they have to hide parts of themselves to be accepted."

The mayor has long been an outspoken critic of the Israeli government and has faced scrutiny from Jewish leaders over his descriptions of Israel, Zionism and organizations that support the Jewish state. Critics argue that separating antisemitism from anti-Zionist rhetoric ignores how Jewish identity is experienced by much of the city’s Jewish population.

Rabbi Yosie Levine of The Jewish Center on Manhattan’s Upper West Side thanked the mayor for recognizing the severity of the problem but called for a corresponding change in his language.

"I want to thank the mayor for his commitment to combat antisemitism," Levine told Fox News Digital. "Acknowledging the problem is an important first step."

ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH

item.title: White Sox look to close out Houston Astros in two games after dominant playoff opener
item.description: Sean Burke and Hunter Brown face off as the Chicago White Sox look to eliminate the Houston Astros and close out the best-of-three playoff series.
item.content:encoded:
I've made a case in the past that it seems a bit unfair that you play 162 games only to have one postseason series given to you, and it's a best-of-three. I feel like there should be a minimum of five games for any playoff series. I understand travel concerns and other issues for this opening round, but it just feels too short. The only argument in favor would be that most regular-season series are three games; however, winning two of three in the regular season doesn't mean much. This afternoon, the White Sox look to close out the Astros in two games.

The Chicago White Sox, a team that had lost 100 or more games in each of the past three seasons, made the postseason this year. item.title: WNBA refs miss opportunity to eject A'ja Wilson over meltdown, entering stands
item.description: Las Vegas Aces star Wilson stepped into the Indiana Fever stands to confront a fan during Game 2, but WNBA rules suggest the play warranted an ejection.
item.content:encoded:
Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson only received a technical foul on Tuesday night when she stepped across the baseline and went a few rows deep to address an Indiana Fever fan.

The incident occurred in the fourth quarter of the Aces’ Game 2 loss to the Fever at the Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Wilson drew a blocking foul after Sophie Cunningham stepped in front of her and fell to the court. Cunningham was upset with the call, meanwhile, Wilson was seen yelling and pointing at a fan a few rows from courtside.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The broadcast showed Wilson taking a few steps into the stands. Crew chief Randy Richardson was asked by a pool reporter about the incident.

"So, at that point, A’ja Wilson was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike conduct," Richardson told the reporter when asked what happened with the incident.

When asked, "Why did A’ja Wilson receive a tech for her interaction with the fan on the baseline," Richardson responded, "For unsportsmanlike conduct."

Wilson finished the game, but it appeared the incident may have warranted an ejection.

The league considers the stands the first row of seats. Wilson didn’t climb over anyone to get to the fan she had an issue with, but, on the baseline, she didn’t need to.

"Any coach, player, or trainer who deliberately enters the spectator stands during the game will be automatically ejected and the incident reported via e-mail to the Commissioner," the rulebook states.

OutKick asked the WNBA and National Basketball Referees Association for comment on why Wilson’s action didn’t warrant an ejection. OutKick also asked the WNBA if it would review the incident further.

The Fever released a statement on the incident.

"Following a report of a comment directed toward a player, arena security spoke with the fan involved and witnesses," the team said. "Security determined there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct, the fan was not removed from the arena. We consider the matter closed."

Wilson addressed the confrontation after the game.

"If I see a man, come at me, taking steps toward me and point at me, I don’t give a damn what you said, I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone, that is unacceptable," she said. "You don’t step toward me and point at me. I’m not for that s--- at all.

"That’s unacceptable and how he gets back in the game because they said he didn’t know anything, of course he didn’t, and that’s fine. And I apologized to my team because I got us a tech and I didn’t … but there’s certain things I’m just not gonna allow anymore because it’s just unacceptable. You don’t know me at all to come and step toward me and point at me and say anything."

A fan sitting next to the man in question later told OutKick that the man only said the foul was on Wilson and pointed at her.

As the WNBA has grown more popular, the scrutiny over officiating in the league has come under the microscope and this season was no different.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said last summer the league was going to evolve terms of its officiating. The league formed an offseason officiating task force that included an effort to clean up some of the WNBA’s issues regarding physicality and officiating.

Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve, who blasted officials during last year’s WNBA Finals, said in the beginning of the 2026 season that coaches weren’t looking for referees to call marginal fouls.

New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart and Dallas Wings rookie Azzi Fudd also talked about the fouls. Stewart was annoyed that a game against the Washington Mystics earlier in the year took nearly three hours to complete. Fudd was dismayed about being unable to be physical with opponents.

Fever star Caitlin Clark went as far as to call for full-time WNBA referees as she racked up technical fouls this season that nearly cost her a game.

"It's kind of been a discussion for three years now, and I think we really need to do a better job protecting the people in this league," she said in July. "I've been involved in a few of those plays, but there's been plenty of others across the league that haven't been called. You go back postgame or whatever it is, teams submit clips and nothing changes. I think overall the league has to do better."

"Overall, the league just has to do better and we have to invest in those areas," she added. "The technology can get better. We can treat the referees a little bit better. Pay them like they're full-time employees."

With the rules already in place, one has to wonder why Wilson wasn’t ejected from Tuesday night’s game.

DALLAS — A competitive Senate race is testing whether Texas is still safely red, with Black and Hispanic voters at the center of Democrat James Talarico's path to victory.

Talarico is seeking to become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win a statewide race in the Lone Star State.

"I definitely do think, if there’s any time for Texas to get a Democrat elected, this is the time to strike," Mike, a military veteran from Dallas, told Fox News Digital. "I think it depends on whether the Black and Brown voters come out for Talarico."

Mike’s comments reflect the challenge facing Talarico as he works to build support among Black and Hispanic voters and motivate them to turn out in November.

Texas has more Black eligible voters than any other state, with roughly 2.7 million. That puts voters in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth and East Texas in a potentially decisive position in any Democrat’s bid to win statewide.

Former President Barack Obama’s appearance with Talarico at a May campaign stop in Austin underscored the stakes for Democrats to leverage a massive voting bloc in Texas. The party's effort to win over Black voters could help determine whether Texas remains reliably red or becomes more competitive for Democrats in future elections.

But Talarico faces an uphill battle in uniting Democrats behind his campaign after a divisive primary against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. Talarico defeated Crockett in the Democratic primary earlier this year, and the outgoing congresswoman has not endorsed his Senate campaign.

Crockett has said she supports the Democratic ticket in Texas, but her political action committee has not endorsed Talarico or campaigned for him.

Rashaun, of Forney, Texas, said the primary loss may have left some Black voters frustrated.

"Everyone was behind Jasmine," Rashaun said. "So that’s what’s blocking, I’m going to say for my people, that was blocking their minds."

Still, Rashaun said she plans to vote for Talarico and hopes Texas will turn blue in November.

"Yes, we are voting in November and it’s going to be Talarico," she said. "We need Texas to flip. We can wish and hope and pray. But we need to get out and vote."

"Right now it is on the Texas voters to get out and support James Talarico or sit at home if you don’t want to see that change," he said.

Bryant, of Coppell, Texas, likewise pointed to frustration with Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton, both Republicans, as a potential motivator for people to support Talarico's candidacy.

Ava, a college student from Denton, said Talarico’s outreach to younger voters has helped him connect with a generation that often feels overlooked.

"I do think he’s going to pull through," she said. "He engages with the younger community, which is important because we feel like we’re not represented."

She added that his social media presence has also helped younger voters connect with his campaign. She first learned about Talarico after meeting him at the Texas State Fair last year and later followed him online.

item.description: Bodycam footage showed four children hiding in a bathroom after Nathalie Belizaire allegedly left them alone to board the Carnival Conquest.
item.content:encoded:
A Florida mother is facing four felony charges after allegedly abandoning her four young children — including a 2-month-old infant — to take a three-day vacation on a cruise ship to the Bahamas.

Nathalie Belizaire, 29, was charged with four counts of child neglect after she boarded Carnival Cruise Line’s Carnival Conquest, leaving her children unattended in her North Miami Beach residence. Police said U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers took her into custody Monday as she disembarked.

"You cannot make this up," Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mindy Glazer said in Tuesday court footage. "We are just grateful nothing worse happened to those kids.

"Who leaves four little kids alone to go on a cruise?

The children were discovered by police Saturday, the day after the ship set sail. Bodycam footage showed four kids coming out of hiding in a bathroom – a 2-year-old toddler, a pre-teen and what appeared to be a teenage girl holding a newborn baby.

Lether Bazile, the father of the 2-month-old, told police that Belizaire claimed she was leaving the children with their great-grandmother, the New York Post reported.

The father was tipped off by the mother's absence by Belizaire’s WhatsApp story two days earlier that appeared to show a Carnival Cruise Line ticket, he told police.

He immediately called the police, who entered the home and found the four children hiding in a bathroom with no adult present.

According to authorities, the children's grandmother, Denise Wilkes, told officers that Belizaire had promised to drop the kids off but never showed up. "At this time, it is only an allegation; she denies the allegation," the defense attorney said.

"Of course she does," Glazer said as the accused showed exasperation.

"They arrested her disembarking from the cruise ship!" the judge then shot back.

TWO MISSING CHILDREN RESCUED FROM TRAILER AS POLICE ARREST BABYSITTER ON KIDNAPPING CHARGES

"There are also others responsible, it's not just mothers," the defense attorney replied. "It's not just mothers that are in charge of children, judge. It's also fathers and grandparents and other people."

Belizaire was given a stay away order until the Department of Children and Families can investigate. She faces four felony counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. Bond was set at $10,000, $2,500 per child.

item.title: Astros players call out fans for booing during Game 1 loss to White Sox: 'Extremely frustrating'
item.description: Houston Astros players blasted fans for booing and empty seats at Daikin Park during their Wild Card Series Game 1 loss to the Chicago White Sox.
item.content:encoded:
The Houston Astros head into Wednesday with their season on the line after losing Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series to the Chicago White Sox, but it’s not their opponent they were mad about.

It was their own fan base.

The Astros, who came into this MLB postseason as baseball’s first-ever division winner with a .500 or worse record, entered Daikin Park in Houston to see a pretty empty stadium in comparison to past playoff matchups.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It was quite noticeable, especially in the upper deck, that there were loads of empty seats. Daikin Park eventually announced an attendance of 34,011, with the ballpark holding a capacity of 40,963.

Could it have been the 4:10 p.m. local-time first pitch on a Tuesday? That could certainly be a factor, as MLB spaces these Wild Card Series games out for national viewing purposes despite odd weekday times that cut into a usual workday.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Either way, Astros players were not happy when they started hearing boos rain down onto the field as the White Sox took an early lead on the road.

"It’s extremely frustrating as a home player," Astros first baseman Christian Walker admitted to The Athletic about hearing jeers from the home crowd. "We’re here, playing at home; we need cheers. We need energy. We don’t need boos. What purpose does that serve in that moment? Whatever fans are feeling, we’re feeling it tenfold. We’re the ones out there. We’re the ones in the fight. We worked our butts off this whole season to put ourselves in this spot, and for guys to get booed, it’s frustrating."

Chicago ended up taking Game 1, 6-3, in a contest that saw both teams put together a bullpen game, which favored the White Sox in the end.

One of those relievers for the Astros was Bennett Sousa, who heard boos from the crowd in the top of the seventh inning when he spiked two breaking balls.

"This team has laid a lot on the line to be in this position to give the fans a playoff game – a playoff series. We want their support," Sousa added, via the outlet.

It may not have been the best year for the Astros, but in an odd AL West division, their 81-81 record was enough to take the crown. It marked the ninth time in the last 10 years Houston has made it to the playoffs, and in that span, they’ve reached the World Series four times, winning in a controversial 2017 season due to their uncovering sign-stealing scandal, and in 2022.

The Astros were 14th this season in attendance at Daikin Park, averaging just over 30,000 fans per game.

Once again, the Astros will play at 4 p.m. local time in Houston, with Hunter Brown getting the ball. He will face Sean Burke on the mound for the White Sox.

item.title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife Anna share heartbreaking news of the death of their baby boy
item.description: Eli Raridon's wife Anna shared a heartbreaking message about losing their baby boy to anencephaly, a rare condition affecting 1 in 4,762 births.
item.content:encoded:
New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon will report to work on Wednesday, almost definitely with a heavy heart.

The rookie out of Notre Dame and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced Tuesday that they lost their baby boy to anencephaly, a fatal birth defect that stops the forebrain and cerebrum from forming in the womb.

There is no cure or standard treatment for the condition. About 75% of affected pregnancies end in stillbirth. Infants born alive usually pass away within a few hours or days.

Devastating.

RAIDERS' AIDAN O'CONNELL ANNOUNCES DEATH OF HIS FATHER, LEANING ON FAITH IN TIME OF SORROW

"When Eli and I went in for our 20-week anatomy scan, excited to see our sweet baby boy, our hearts were forever changed," Anna wrote on her Instagram account. "Our little one was diagnosed with anencephaly, a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.

"While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven."

What comes next is a mother who, rather than getting lost in the unspeakable pain of losing a baby, chose to lean into her faith during a time of deep tribulation.

"I have often found it easy to glorify the Lord when life is going well, but it is in our deepest trials that we are drawn closest to Him," Anna continued. "We may never understand the why behind this journey, but one thing we know with certainty is that God promises to care for His children.

"I believe our little boy was lovingly knitted together in the womb by God, knowing how deeply he would be loved by our families, our friends, Eli, and me. Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story."

And then the Raridons left a message for their baby boy:

"I have loved you every second of your life and will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be🤍"

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

The CDC Data and Statistics on Birth Defects reports that about 1 in every 4,762 is born with anencephaly. That is roughly .02% of live births.

But while the defect is not necessarily common it is quite personal. Literature states that the recurrence rate after one pregnancy is affected by anencephaly jumps dramatically to between 2%-5%.

And while that means there is a 95%-98% chance the Raridons will never be touched by this condition again, their concern must be real.

Anna Raridon shared Scripture she is leaning on to get her through this terrible time:

1 Peter 1:5-7: "who by God’s power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith – more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire – may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ."

And this:‭‭

James 1:2-4: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing."

item.title: USMNT gets into bench-clearing brawl after Chilean player kicks at goalkeeper in closing seconds of friendly
item.description: A bench-clearing brawl capped the USMNT-Chile friendly in St. Louis, with Mauricio Pochettino caught in the chaos four years from the World Cup.
item.content:encoded:
International friendlies in late September nearly four full years out from the next World Cup typically leave a lot to be desired, but that was not the case on Tuesday with the U.S. men's national team playing host to Chile in St. Louis.

The match entered the break knotted at 1-1 before the two sides traded goals just six minutes into the second half. The USMNT was able to break the tie courtesy of a Chris Richards goal in the 72nd minute before 17-year-old Mathis Albert added some cushion with a tally in the 93rd minute to secure a 4-2 victory.

While it seemed likely that Albert's goal in stoppage time would be the final noteworthy moment of the match, that was very much not the case.

Nearly a full minute beyond the five minutes of allotted stoppage time had come off the clock; USMNT goalkeeper Brian Schwake fell on a loose ball, looking to milk the final seconds of the contest.

Chilean forward Leandro Hernandez continued his jog towards Schwake and appeared to take a small kick at the ball. Richards saw Hernandez's kick at the ball, took exception, and within seconds every player on the field was pushing and shoving.

The benches cleared with personnel from both teams sprinting onto the pitch, and that included USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was caught right in the middle of the altercation.

"It’s a crazy situation," Pochettino said after the final whistle. "You try to divide the players and calm down. Sometimes, when you are winning you have to understand the opponent may go to the line and walk over the line in frustration."

USMNT midfielder Tyler Adams was the most animated of the bunch as cameras caught him pointing towards Chilean players shouting at them while being held back by teammates.
